lessons.title: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost
lessons.objective: Explain scarcity, choice and opportunity cost, and rank competing wants with a scale of preference.

content.heading: The economic problem
paragraphs: Economics begins with a mismatch: human wants are unlimited, but the resources used to satisfy them are limited. That gap is scarcity, and it forces everyone — households, firms and governments — to choose.
bullets: Scarcity means resources are insufficient to satisfy every want at once. It is not the same as shortage, which is temporary.
Because resources are scarce, choosing one use means giving up another.
A scale of preference ranks wants in order of importance, so limited income goes to the most pressing wants first.
Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone — not the money paid.

content.heading: How societies answer three questions
paragraphs: Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. The way it answers those questions defines its economic system.
bullets: Free enterprise (capitalist): private individuals own the factors of production and prices coordinate most decisions.
Centrally planned (socialist): the government owns and directs resources through a plan.
Mixed economy: markets and government both allocate resources. Nigeria is a mixed economy — private firms dominate production while government regulates and provides public goods.
The production possibility frontier shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce; a point inside the curve is inefficient.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Opportunity cost is the alternative you gave up, not the naira you spent. If you spend N2,000 on data instead of a textbook, the opportunity cost is the textbook.

content.problem: A student has N2,000. She ranks a textbook first, a data bundle second and a cinema ticket third. She buys the textbook. What is her opportunity cost?

steps.reason: Opportunity cost is measured against what was actually chosen.
steps.result: She chose the textbook.
steps.predictPrompt: Which want came next on her scale of preference?

steps.reason: Only the highest-ranked forgone option counts, not every option she skipped.
steps.result: The data bundle is the next best alternative.

steps.reason: The N2,000 is the money cost; it is not the forgone alternative.
steps.result: Opportunity cost = the data bundle she did not buy.

content.question: Nigeria is usually described as a mixed economy. Name one decision left mainly to markets and one left mainly to government, then explain why scarcity makes the choice necessary.
hints: Markets decide most prices and what private firms produce; government provides defence, roads and regulates utilities.
Scarcity means not every want can be met, so someone must decide which wants come first.
A strong answer links the two sectors to the three questions — what, how and for whom — and names opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Demand, Supply and Equilibrium
lessons.objective: Apply the laws of demand and supply, distinguish shifts from movements, and solve for equilibrium price and quantity.

content.heading: Demand and its determinants
paragraphs: The law of demand says that, all else equal, quantity demanded falls as price rises. The demand curve therefore slopes downward.
bullets: A change in the good’s own price moves you along the demand curve — a change in quantity demanded.
A change in income, tastes, population, expectations or the price of a related good shifts the whole curve — a change in demand.
Normal goods: demand rises with income. Inferior goods: demand falls as income rises.
Types of demand: complementary (used together), competitive (substitutes), composite (one good, many uses), derived (demand for a factor from demand for its product).

content.heading: Supply and equilibrium
paragraphs: The law of supply says quantity supplied rises with price, so the supply curve slopes upward. Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
bullets: Above equilibrium price there is a surplus, which pushes price down.
Below equilibrium price there is a shortage, which pushes price up.
An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and quantity; an increase in supply lowers price and raises quantity.
Elasticity measures how strongly quantity responds to price; demand is elastic when the percentage change in quantity exceeds the percentage change in price.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Own price moves you along the curve. Every other determinant shifts the curve. Read the question for which one changed.

content.problem: Given Qd = 15 − 2P and Qs = 5 + 3P, find the equilibrium price and quantity.

steps.operation: Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied
steps.reason: At equilibrium the market clears, so Qd = Qs.
steps.predictPrompt: How do you collect the P terms on one side?

steps.reason: Subtract 5 from both sides and add 2P to both sides.
Either equation gives the equilibrium quantity at P = 2.
steps.result: Qd = 15 − 2(2) = 11, and Qs = 5 + 3(2) = 11. Equilibrium is P = 2, Q = 11.

content.question: The price of petrol rises. Explain why this shifts the demand curve for large cars rather than moving along it.
hints: Petrol is not the price of the car itself; it is the price of a complementary good used with the car.
A change in the price of a complement changes demand at every car price, so the whole curve shifts left.
A strong answer distinguishes the own-price movement from a shift caused by a related good.

lessons.title: Production, Factors and Diminishing Returns
lessons.objective: Match each factor of production to its reward and explain why marginal product eventually falls.

content.heading: Factors of production and their rewards
paragraphs: Production combines four factors of production. Each is paid a reward that reflects its contribution.
bullets: Land — all natural resources; reward is rent.
Labour — human effort, physical and mental; reward is wages or salaries.
Capital — man-made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines and buildings; reward is interest.
Entrepreneurship — organises the other factors and bears risk; reward is profit (which can be negative).
Division of labour splits work into specialised tasks. It raises output per worker but can cause boredom, over-dependence and coordination costs.

content.heading: Diminishing returns and costs
paragraphs: In the short run at least one factor is fixed. Adding more of a variable factor to it eventually yields smaller extra output — the law of diminishing returns.
bullets: Marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of the variable factor.
Diminishing returns sets in when marginal product starts to fall, even though total output may still be rising.
Fixed costs do not change with output (rent, machinery). Variable costs do (raw materials, hourly labour).
Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Marginal product falls before total product does. Total output can keep rising while each extra worker adds less than the one before.

content.problem: A farm has fixed land. With 1, 2, 3 and 4 workers, total output is 10, 25, 35 and 40 tonnes. At which worker do diminishing returns set in?

steps.reason: Marginal product is the change in total output when one more worker is added.
steps.result: MP = 10, 15, 10, 5 tonnes for workers 1–4.
steps.predictPrompt: Which is the first fall in marginal product?

steps.reason: Diminishing returns begin when marginal product turns downward.
steps.result: MP rises from 10 to 15, then falls to 10 at the third worker.

steps.reason: The third worker adds less than the second, so the law has set in.
steps.result: Diminishing returns set in at the third worker, even though total output rises to 35 tonnes.

content.question: A bakery pays N200,000 a month in rent and N5,000 per worker per day. Classify each cost and explain what happens to average fixed cost as output rises.
hints: Rent is paid whether or not bread is baked, so it is fixed. Daily wages vary with the number of workers, so they are variable.
Average fixed cost is fixed cost divided by output.
A strong answer notes that average fixed cost falls as output rises, while average variable cost may fall and then rise.

lessons.title: Market Structures
lessons.objective: Distinguish perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition by sellers, products and entry.

content.heading: Perfect competition
paragraphs: Perfect competition is a benchmark market with many small firms selling an identical product. No single firm can influence the market price.
bullets: Many buyers and many sellers, each too small to affect price.
Homogeneous (identical) products, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
Free entry and exit, and perfect information about prices.
The firm is a price taker: its demand curve is horizontal at the market price.

content.heading: Imperfect markets
paragraphs: When a firm can influence price, the market is imperfect. The three main forms differ by how many firms there are and whether products are differentiated.
bullets: Monopoly: one seller, no close substitute, high barriers to entry; the firm is a price maker.
Oligopoly: a few large firms whose decisions depend on one another; advertising and non-price competition are common.
Monopolistic competition: many firms selling differentiated products, with easy entry.
A monopsony is the mirror image — one buyer facing many sellers.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Ask three questions: how many sellers, is the product identical or differentiated, and can new firms enter? Those three answers identify almost every market structure.

content.problem: A single firm supplies electricity to a city and no other firm can enter the market. Which market structure is this, and why does government usually regulate its price?

steps.reason: One seller is the defining feature of monopoly.
steps.result: The market is a monopoly.

steps.reason: Electricity has no close substitute for most users, and the grid is a natural barrier to entry.
steps.result: The firm can set price without competitive pressure.

steps.reason: A price-making monopolist may restrict output and charge high prices.
steps.result: Government regulates the tariff to protect consumers while allowing the firm to cover costs.

content.question: Why do firms in an oligopoly advertise heavily while perfectly competitive firms do not?
hints: Perfectly competitive firms sell identical products at the market price, so advertising cannot raise their price.
Oligopolists sell differentiated products and compete for market share; advertising can shift demand toward them.
A strong answer links advertising to product differentiation and interdependence.

lessons.title: Money and Inflation
lessons.objective: Name the functions and qualities of money and distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation.

content.heading: Functions and qualities of money
paragraphs: Money is anything generally accepted as a means of payment. It removes the double coincidence of wants that makes barter difficult.
bullets: Functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Qualities: generally acceptable, divisible, portable, durable, homogeneous and limited in supply.
Homogeneity matters because every unit must be identical, so values can be counted and compared.
Anything that fails these qualities — cattle, cowries, cocoa — is a poor money even if it is valuable.

content.heading: Inflation
paragraphs: Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money. Deflation is the opposite.
bullets: Demand-pull inflation: aggregate demand grows faster than output.
Cost-push inflation: rising costs of inputs such as fuel, wages or imported raw materials push prices up.
Imported inflation: higher prices of imported goods enter the domestic price level.
Fixed-income earners, savers and creditors lose purchasing power; borrowers gain because debts are repaid in cheaper money.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Demand-pull starts with buyers; cost-push starts with sellers’ costs. Excess demand over supply is always demand-pull.

content.problem: Government pays a large cash transfer, households spend it quickly, but output is unchanged. Which type of inflation follows, and who loses most?

steps.reason: The extra spending raises aggregate demand, while output has not risen.
steps.result: Demand exceeds supply, so prices are pulled up.
steps.predictPrompt: Does this originate with buyers or with costs?

steps.reason: Inflation caused by excess demand is demand-pull.
steps.result: The economy experiences demand-pull inflation.

steps.reason: People whose incomes are fixed in naira can buy less as prices rise.
steps.result: Fixed-income earners and savers lose the most; borrowers gain.

content.question: A farmer’s diesel, fertiliser and transport costs all rise, and food prices follow. Identify the inflation type and one policy response, noting its limitation.
hints: The increase begins on the cost side, not with excess demand.
A central bank can raise interest rates to reduce demand, but that does not lower fuel or fertiliser costs directly.
A strong answer names cost-push inflation and explains the trade-off between fighting inflation and protecting output.

lessons.title: International Trade and Comparative Advantage
lessons.objective: Explain the gains from trade, compute opportunity cost, and distinguish the terms of trade from the balances.

content.heading: Why countries trade
paragraphs: Countries trade because they differ in resources, technology and costs. Specialising where opportunity cost is lowest raises total output, and both sides can gain.
bullets: Absolute advantage: a country can produce more of a good with the same resources.
Comparative advantage: a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost. This, not absolute advantage, is the basis of beneficial trade.
David Ricardo showed that even a country that is better at everything gains by specialising where its disadvantage is smallest.
Other gains: economies of scale, wider consumer choice and access to goods a country cannot produce.

content.heading: Terms of trade and the balances
paragraphs: The terms of trade measure the rate at which exports exchange for imports. The two balances measure different things and are often confused.
bullets: Terms of trade = (index of export prices ÷ index of import prices) × 100. A rise means exports buy more imports.
Balance of trade = visible exports − visible imports. It covers goods only.
Balance of payments = all receipts and payments, including services, income and transfers. It can balance even when trade does not.
Invisible trade covers services such as banking, shipping, insurance and tourism.
ECOWAS promotes trade and free movement among West African states; its slow progress is often blamed on weak political will and inadequate resources.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A trade deficit is not the same as a payments deficit. Services, remittances and capital inflows can close a goods gap.

content.problem: With the same resources, Country A can produce 10 tonnes of cocoa or 5 tonnes of coffee; Country B can produce 4 tonnes of cocoa or 8 tonnes of coffee. Who should produce which?

steps.reason: Giving up 10 cocoa frees resources for 5 coffee, so 1 coffee costs 2 cocoa.
steps.result: A: 1 coffee = 2 cocoa, or 1 cocoa = 0.5 coffee.
steps.predictPrompt: Now do the same for B.

steps.reason: Giving up 4 cocoa frees resources for 8 coffee, so 1 coffee costs 0.5 cocoa.
steps.result: B: 1 coffee = 0.5 cocoa, or 1 cocoa = 2 coffee.

steps.reason: Each country should produce the good for which it gives up less.
steps.result: A has the lower cocoa cost (0.5 coffee vs 2), so A produces cocoa; B has the lower coffee cost (0.5 cocoa vs 2), so B produces coffee.

content.question: Explain dumping and one reason it harms local producers, then name one trade remedy a government could use.
hints: Dumping is selling exports below home cost or below the price charged at home.
Foreign goods priced below local production cost can take market share and force local firms to cut prices or close.
A government can impose an anti-dumping duty or a tariff to raise the imported price.

lessons.title: Utility, Diminishing Marginal Utility and Consumer Choice
lessons.objective: Distinguish total, average and marginal utility, apply diminishing marginal utility, and compute consumer surplus.

content.heading: Utility and the margin
paragraphs: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer derives from a good. It is subjective: the same good can give different satisfaction to different people, or to the same person at different times.
bullets: Total utility (TU) is the satisfaction from all units consumed.
Average utility is total utility divided by the number of units.
Marginal utility (MU) is the extra satisfaction from one more unit.
The law of diminishing marginal utility says MU falls as consumption of a good increases in a given period.
Total utility is maximised when MU = 0; a negative MU reduces total utility.

content.heading: Consumer surplus and indifference curves
paragraphs: Consumers often pay less than the maximum they were willing to pay. That gap is consumer surplus, and it is one reason market exchange creates gains.
bullets: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price actually paid.
An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give equal total satisfaction.
A budget line shows the combinations a consumer can afford at given prices and income.
Consumer equilibrium occurs where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the budget line.
The water–diamond paradox: water is vital but cheap because its marginal utility is low; diamonds are frivolous but expensive because their marginal utility is high.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Utility is satisfaction, not usefulness. A useless ornament can give high utility, while a useful tool may give little.

content.problem: A student’s total utility from 1, 2, 3 and 4 bottles of water is 10, 18, 24 and 28. Find the marginal utility of each bottle, and say where diminishing marginal utility begins.

steps.reason: MU is the change in total utility from one more unit.
steps.result: MU = 10, 8, 6 and 4 for bottles 1–4.
steps.predictPrompt: Is marginal utility rising or falling?

steps.reason: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less than the previous one.
steps.result: MU falls from 10 to 8 at the second bottle, so the law applies from there.

steps.reason: TU is still rising because every MU is positive.
steps.result: TU rises to 28; it would stop rising only when MU reaches zero.

content.question: A thirsty student drinks three bottles of water. Explain why the third may give less satisfaction than the first, and what happens to total utility if a fourth bottle makes her sick.
hints: The first bottle removes the strongest thirst; later bottles meet weaker wants.
A bottle that makes her sick has negative marginal utility.
A strong answer says total utility falls when marginal utility turns negative.

lessons.title: National Income and Its Measurement
lessons.objective: Define GDP and GNP, convert nominal to real income, compute per capita income, and explain what is excluded.

content.heading: Measuring output
paragraphs: National income is the total value of goods and services produced in an economy over a year. It can be measured by output, income or expenditure, and the three should agree.
bullets: GDP counts output produced within a country’s borders, whoever owns the producer.
GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad. It counts income earned by a country’s citizens.
The expenditure approach adds consumption, investment, government spending and net exports: C + I + G + (X − M).
Only final goods are counted; intermediate goods would double-count the same output.
Transfer payments, second-hand sales and purely financial transactions are excluded because they create no new output.

content.heading: Real income, per capita income and development
paragraphs: Nominal income is measured at current prices; real income is measured at constant prices, so it shows whether output actually grew.
bullets: Real GDP = (nominal GDP ÷ price index) × 100.
Per capita income = national income ÷ population. It is an average, so it hides inequality.
Economic growth is a sustained rise in real output; economic development also includes health, education and structural change.
A rise in nominal GDP can be pure inflation, so it is not proof of better living standards.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: GDP is about where output is produced; GNP is about who earns the income. Read the question for “within the country” versus “by citizens”.

content.problem: Nominal GDP is N200 billion, the price index is 125, and the population is 40 million. Find real GDP and per capita real income.

steps.reason: Divide by the price index and multiply by 100 to remove price changes.
steps.result: Real GDP = (200 ÷ 125) × 100 = N160 billion.
steps.predictPrompt: Now divide by population — in what units?

steps.reason: Per capita income is national income per person.
steps.result: N160 billion ÷ 40 million = N4,000 per person.

steps.reason: The average is not a measure of distribution.
steps.result: Average real income is N4,000; many people may still be far below it.

content.question: Why is a rise in nominal GDP not proof that living standards improved? Give two reasons.
hints: Prices may have risen, so the same output is worth more in naira.
Population may have grown faster, leaving income per head unchanged or lower.
A strong answer also mentions distribution and unpaid/non-market production.

lessons.title: Financial Institutions and the Central Bank
lessons.objective: Distinguish the Central Bank, deposit money banks and development banks, and explain the CBN’s main functions.

content.heading: The banking system
paragraphs: Financial institutions move funds from savers to borrowers. The Central Bank sits at the top, with commercial and development banks below it.
bullets: Deposit money banks (commercial banks) accept deposits, create credit and lend, mainly short term.
Development banks supply medium- and long-term finance for agriculture, industry and infrastructure.
Merchant banks handle wholesale banking and corporate finance.
Microfinance banks serve small borrowers who cannot meet commercial-bank collateral requirements.
Non-bank institutions include insurance companies and pension funds.

content.heading: Functions of the Central Bank
paragraphs: The CBN is the apex financial institution. It does not compete with commercial banks for retail customers; it regulates and supports them.
bullets: Issues currency notes and coins.
Acts as banker to the federal government and manages its accounts.
Acts as banker to banks and lender of last resort.
Formulates and implements monetary policy, including interest rates and reserve requirements.
Manages external reserves and the exchange rate, and supervises banks.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: The CBN is banker to the government and to the banks. A commercial bank is banker to the public.

content.problem: A commercial bank faces a sudden wave of withdrawals and cannot borrow from other banks. Who can help it, and under which function?

steps.operation: Identify the lender of last resort
steps.reason: When no other bank will lend, the apex bank can provide emergency liquidity.
steps.result: The Central Bank of Nigeria can lend to it.
steps.predictPrompt: Why not let the bank fail?

steps.reason: This is the CBN’s lender-of-last-resort role, part of its financial-stability mandate.
steps.result: The CBN acts as lender of last resort.

steps.reason: Emergency lending is not free money; the bank must be solvent and provide collateral.
steps.result: Support is temporary and supervised, to stop panic without rewarding bad management.

content.question: A new factory needs finance for ten years. Distinguish what the CBN and a development bank can each do.
hints: The CBN sets monetary policy and supports the banking system; it does not normally lend to individual firms.
Development banks provide long-term project finance, often at concessional rates.
A strong answer says the CBN creates the environment and the development bank supplies the loan.

lessons.title: Government Revenue, Taxation and the Budget
lessons.objective: Classify taxes, explain budget outcomes, and distinguish fiscal policy from monetary policy.

content.heading: Government revenue and spending
paragraphs: Public finance studies how government raises and spends money. Revenue comes from oil and non-oil sources; spending is recurrent or capital.
bullets: Revenue: taxes, fees, licences, fines, dividends from state enterprises, grants, aid and borrowing.
Recurrent expenditure: salaries, allowances, debt service and day-to-day running costs.
Capital expenditure: roads, schools, hospitals, power and other long-term assets.
Borrowing is not revenue in the true sense; it creates a future obligation.

content.heading: Taxes and the budget
paragraphs: A tax is a compulsory payment to government. Taxes can be classified by how they are collected and by how the burden falls.
bullets: Direct tax: levied on income or wealth, e.g. personal income tax and company tax.
Indirect tax: levied on goods and services, e.g. VAT, import duty and excise duty.
Progressive tax: the rate rises with income. Proportional: the same rate. Regressive: the rate falls as income rises.
Budget surplus: revenue exceeds expenditure. Deficit: expenditure exceeds revenue. Balanced: the two are equal.
Fiscal policy uses taxation and government spending; monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: VAT is indirect even though the seller hands it over. The tax is on the sale, and the seller passes it to government.

content.problem: Classify each tax and say whether it is direct or indirect: personal income tax, VAT, import duty, company tax.

steps.reason: Direct taxes fall on income or wealth; indirect taxes fall on goods and services.
steps.result: Personal income tax and company tax are direct; VAT and import duty are indirect.
steps.predictPrompt: Who ultimately bears the burden of VAT?

steps.reason: VAT is collected by sellers but added to prices.
steps.result: Consumers bear most of the VAT burden, which is why it can be regressive.

steps.reason: Import duty is charged on imported goods, so it is indirect.
steps.result: Direct: personal income tax, company tax. Indirect: VAT, import duty.

content.question: Government wants to reduce a budget deficit without cutting capital projects. Name two options and one risk of each.
hints: It can raise tax revenue or cut recurrent spending.
It can also borrow, but that adds debt-service costs and may crowd out private investment.
A strong answer notes the trade-off between short-term relief and long-term growth.

lessons.title: Agriculture, Industry and the Oil Sector
lessons.objective: Explain agriculture’s role, the factors that locate industry, and the difference between upstream and downstream oil.

content.heading: Agriculture
paragraphs: Agriculture supplies food, employs labour and provides raw materials for industry. In Nigeria it remains the largest employer even though oil dominates foreign exchange.
bullets: Provides food and improves food security.
Employs a large share of the population.
Supplies raw materials to agro-processing industries.
Earns foreign exchange through cash crops and provides a market for industrial goods.
Problems: low mechanisation, insecure land tenure, weak credit, poor storage and transport, and climate risk.

content.heading: Industry and the oil sector
paragraphs: Industrial location depends on costs. Firms balance proximity to raw materials, markets, power, transport, labour and government incentives.
bullets: A weight-losing industry locates near its raw material; a weight-gaining or bulky product locates near its market.
Upstream oil: exploration and extraction of crude oil.
Downstream oil: refining, distribution and marketing of petroleum products.
Over-dependence on oil exposes the economy to price shocks, neglects agriculture and manufacturing, and can cause Dutch disease.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Upstream is finding and extracting; downstream is refining and selling. Refining is never upstream.

content.problem: A cement factory locates beside a limestone deposit rather than in the city. Which location factor dominates, and what trade-off does the firm accept?

steps.reason: Limestone is bulky and expensive to transport, so proximity lowers cost.
steps.result: The firm is raw-material oriented.
steps.predictPrompt: What does it give up by moving away from customers?

steps.reason: Locating near the deposit raises the distance to the market.
steps.result: The firm accepts higher transport costs for finished cement.

steps.reason: The choice depends on which transport cost is larger.
steps.result: When the raw material loses weight in processing, locating near the deposit usually wins.

content.question: Name two ways over-dependence on oil weakens the Nigerian economy.
hints: Oil prices are volatile, so revenue and the exchange rate swing with them.
Easy oil revenue can crowd out agriculture and manufacturing, and imported goods can make local production uncompetitive.
A strong answer mentions price shocks and the neglect of other sectors (or Dutch disease).

lessons.title: Business Organisations
lessons.objective: Compare sole proprietorships, partnerships, companies and co-operatives on ownership, liability and finance.

content.heading: Unincorporated businesses
paragraphs: A sole proprietorship has one owner; a partnership has two to twenty. Neither is a separate legal person from its owners.
bullets: Sole proprietorship: easy and cheap to start, owner keeps all profit, but has unlimited liability and limited capital.
Partnership: pooled capital and skills, shared workload, but unlimited liability and possible disagreement.
Unlimited liability means business debts can be recovered from the owner’s personal assets.
Both end when the owner dies or leaves, so they lack perpetual succession.

content.heading: Companies and co-operatives
paragraphs: Incorporation creates a separate legal person. The company owns assets, signs contracts and bears liability in its own name.
bullets: Private limited company: shares restricted, often family-owned, limited liability, separate legal entity.
Public limited company: shares freely transferable and traded, can raise large capital, subject to stricter disclosure.
Both companies have perpetual succession: they continue when shareholders change.
Co-operative: owned and controlled by members, usually one member one vote, surplus shared according to members’ patronage.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Incorporation is the dividing line. A company is a separate legal person; a sole trader is not.

content.problem: Two friends need N50 million and want to limit their personal risk. Which business form should they choose, and why not a partnership?

steps.reason: A partnership leaves owners personally liable for business debts.
steps.result: A partnership does not cap personal risk.
steps.predictPrompt: Which form limits liability and can raise outside capital?

steps.reason: A limited liability company is a separate legal person and can issue shares.
steps.result: A private limited company fits; it can later become public to raise more capital.

steps.reason: Incorporation brings registration, disclosure and compliance costs.
steps.result: They accept formalities in exchange for limited liability and easier capital raising.

content.question: Why might a co-operative charge members lower prices than a private shop selling the same goods?
hints: A co-operative is owned by its members, not by outside shareholders seeking maximum profit.
Any surplus is returned to members, so the effective price is lower.
A strong answer links ownership and surplus distribution to the price members pay.

lessons.title: Population, Census and the Labour Force
lessons.objective: Interpret population structure, explain the uses of a census, and calculate dependency and participation ratios.

content.heading: Population structure
paragraphs: Population structure describes how a population is distributed by age, sex, occupation and location. It determines how many people work and how many depend on them.
bullets: Working population (labour force): people of working age who are able and willing to work.
Dependency ratio = dependants ÷ working-age population. Children and the elderly are the main dependants.
A youthful population needs schools and jobs; an ageing population needs health and pension spending.
Migration is pushed by low wages, insecurity and unemployment, and pulled by jobs and services.

content.heading: Census and planning
paragraphs: A census is an official count of a country’s population. Accurate figures are a planning tool, not just a statistic.
bullets: Uses: planning schools, hospitals, housing, roads and jobs; allocating revenue; estimating the labour force; delimiting constituencies.
Problems: cost, illiteracy, difficult terrain, religious and ethnic sensitivity, poor logistics and political manipulation.
A census counts people; a survey samples them. Both need clear definitions to be comparable.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: The labour force excludes people of working age who are not able or willing to work — full-time students, retirees and some carers.

content.problem: A country has 120 million people: 45 million under 15, 5 million over 64, and a labour force of 50 million. Find the working-age population, the dependency ratio and the participation rate.

steps.reason: Subtract the dependent age groups from the total.
steps.result: 120 − 45 − 5 = 70 million people of working age.
steps.predictPrompt: Which group is counted as dependants?

steps.reason: Dependants are the under-15 and over-64 groups: 45 + 5 = 50 million.
steps.result: 50 ÷ 70 ≈ 0.71 dependants per working-age person.

steps.reason: The labour force is those working or actively seeking work, not everyone of working age.
steps.result: 50 ÷ 70 ≈ 71.4% participation.

content.question: How can a country’s population grow while its labour force falls? Give two reasons.
hints: Population growth can come from children, who do not join the labour force for years.
More young people staying in school, more retirements, or emigration can shrink the labour force.
A strong answer separates total population from the number able and willing to work.
